query: For a high-entropy alloy designed as a single-phase solid solution and exhibiting a favorable strength–ductility combination, what single testable hypothesis proposes an intervention to preserve toughness after thermal exposure and subsequent loading? Explain the hypothesized mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the same alloy tested under identical conditions without the intervention, define the applicable exposure and loading regime, identify supporting evidence from prior observations, and specify an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of carbon to a high-entropy alloy will preserve toughness after thermal exposure and subsequent loading by promoting a single-phase solid solution and preventing the formation of brittle phases.
generation.conditions: Thermal exposure at 800°C for up to 10 weeks and subsequent loading
generation.mechanism: The addition of carbon promotes a single-phase solid solution, preventing the formation of brittle phases and preserving toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved toughness after thermal exposure and subsequent loading
generation.boundary: Thermal exposure at 800°C for up to 10 weeks and subsequent loading
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism by which carbon addition preserves toughness is not fully understood and may depend on the specific alloy composition and processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the toughness of high-entropy alloys with and without carbon addition after thermal exposure and subsequent loading
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the toughness of the alloy without carbon addition is greater than or equal to the toughness of the alloy with carbon addition, the hypothesis is falsified.

Question: How do simultaneous microalloying with carbon (C) and molybdenum (Mo) affect the microstructure evolution, phase stability, and mechanical properties of Co-Cr-Fe-Ni high-entropy alloys?. System: [Co40Cr25(FeNi)35−yMoy]100−xCx (x = 0, 0.5; y = 3, 4, 5 at.%) HEAs. Processing: Vacuum arc melting of pure elements (≥99.9 wt.%) under Ti-gettered argon atmosphere, melted five times for homogeneity, solution treated at 1200 °C for 2 h, water quenched, and hot rolled with 70% reduction. Test conditions: Room temperature uniaxial tensile testing at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1; XRD (20° to 100°, 40 kV, 40 mA); SEM and EBSD analysis.
